title: Cape Cod
hookLine: he walks the shore and faces the sea's indifference (Cape Cod)

lines: A BOOK THAT OPENS WITH A WRECK.
cards: A book about a beach that begins with a shipwreck.
Thoreau sets out to walk the outer shore of Cape Cod and passes a wreck: a ship broken on the rocks, people from the village searching the sand, wooden boxes laid out for the dead.
He doesn't dress it up, and he doesn't look away. And what stays with him isn't only the boxes. It's the sea itself, which goes on breaking against the shore as if nothing had happened.

teach.h: THE WRECK, AND THE SEA GOING ON.
teach.b: First, the wreck. Thoreau describes the searching and the boxes plainly, with care for the people standing there. Then he notices the waves.
The same sea that broke the ship goes on rolling in, and he doesn't pretend it mourns. Second, no flattery.

teach.h: THERE IS NO FLATTERY IN IT.
teach.b: He calls the seashore a wild, rank place, and says "there is no flattery in it." A garden is arranged for people; a porch view seems laid out for their pleasure.
The outer beach isn't: crabs, weed, wreckage, whatever the water throws up. It isn't against anyone. It simply isn't about them.

Third, neutral ground. He describes the shore as a kind of neutral ground between land and sea, belonging fully to neither, a place where you can't pretend the world was built around you. Fourth, the book's last line.

After all that walking, he stands at the edge and writes, "A man may stand there and put all America behind him." Every argument, town and errand at his back; in front, water that doesn't know his name.
Some readers find that bleak. Others find it a relief: nothing to perform, nobody to impress. This week ran from a jail cell to a wild mountainside, from conscience to contact.
Here at the shore, the whole country is behind him, and the sea doesn't care who he is.

how: Some readers of Thoreau's Cape Cod notice how plainly he looks at the sea, which is neither cruel nor kind; some go to a shore or a wide view to feel how small their own worries look beside it.

games.q: you're Thoreau, on a shore where a ship has just been wrecked. the sea keeps rolling in. what do you write?
o: that the sea is cruel and wicked.
that the sea mourns with the town.

games.why: he doesn't make the sea a villain or a mourner. it simply goes on. the indifference is the point.

practice: Look at the widest view you've got, a skyline, a field, a parking lot, the sky, or close your eyes and bring to mind a sea or a plain you've seen.

Notice that it isn't watching you, grading you or waiting for you to say anything, and let your shoulders drop a little at that. Put one nagging thing behind you, the way Thoreau put the country at his back.
